title: Locking and MVCC in practice
subtitle: Pick the right tool when two requests change the same row, and learn how your database keeps reads fast while rows change.

c.v: On 2 March 2014, a small Bitcoin exchange called Flexcoin lost every coin in its hot wallet. The attacker took 896 BTC. The next day, Flexcoin closed for good.
The attacker did not break in. They created a normal account and deposited some coins. Then they used Flexcoin's feature for transfers between users.

They sent thousands of transfer requests at the same moment. Coins moved out of the sending account "until the sending account was overdrawn, before balances were updated". They repeated this across several accounts to grow the amount, then withdrew it.
Flexcoin did not publish its code. Our reading of the notice: each request checked the balance, then wrote a new balance a moment later. Many requests passed the check before the first writes landed.

First try to make the change one statement. If you must read first, lock when conflicts are common and the lock is short. Check a version when conflicts are rare or a person is thinking.

The big win is time. The read and the write can be minutes apart, in two HTTP requests. No lock is held in between. Martin Fowler's catalog calls this pattern Optimistic Offline Lock. It "assumes that the chance of conflict is low".
For counters and balances you often need no version at all:

MVCC: why readers do not wait
The Postgres docs say it plainly: "reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading".
The trick is that a write keeps the old version of the row for readers who still need it.

It is 0 for an undeleted row. A visible row can still show a number, usually because the deleting transaction has not committed or was rolled back.
The old version stays on disk. It must not be removed "while it is still potentially visible to other transactions".

Plain VACUUM does not usually give space back to the operating system. After a big spike of updates, a table can bloat until you need

Here is the trap. A row version stays while it is "still potentially visible to other transactions".
So, we infer, one transaction left open for hours can stop VACUUM from removing dead versions. This applies to a transaction that holds a snapshot or has written something.

Advisory locks, and beyond one database
Sometimes you want to lock an idea, not a row. For example: "only one nightly billing job runs". Postgres
take a number you choose. The database does not enforce their meaning; your code must ask for them.

BEGIN;
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(4242);  -- true or false, no wait
-- if true: do the work
COMMIT;  -- releases the lock

They are released at the end of the transaction.
Session-level ones stay until you unlock them or the session ends, even after a rollback.
, prefer the transaction-level versions. For a long job, take a session-level lock on one connection that you keep for the whole job, and unlock it at the end. Or use a lock row with an expiry.

q.v: You run UPDATE tickets SET body = $1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3. Postgres answers UPDATE 0. What does it mean?

options.v: The database had an error. Log it and move on.
Someone changed the row after you read it. Reload it, then retry or show a conflict.
The update worked, but Postgres did not count it.

why.v: The version is no longer 3, so no row matched. Postgres does not treat 0 rows as an error, so your code must check the count.

q.v: Ten workers take jobs from one jobs table. Each job must run once, and workers should not wait for each other. Which read fits best?

why.v: SKIP LOCKED passes over rows another worker has locked, so each worker gets a different job at once. The docs name queue-like tables as the use case.

q.v: Someone leaves a Postgres transaction open for six hours. A busy table keeps growing on disk. Why?

options.v: VACUUM cannot remove old row versions that the open transaction might still need to see.
The open transaction holds a lock that blocks all writes.
Autovacuum runs only once a day.

why.v: An old row version must stay while it is still potentially visible to an open transaction. So one old transaction can hold back cleanup of dead versions.

q.v: Two money transfers sometimes fail with "deadlock detected". One locks account 17 then 42, the other 42 then 17. What is the best fix?

options.v: Lock rows in one fixed order, such as lowest ID first, and retry the transaction on a deadlock error.
Remove the transaction so each UPDATE commits alone.

why.v: A consistent lock order removes the wait cycle. A retry handles the rare cases that are left. Removing the transaction breaks atomicity.

q.v: Users edit a product description in a form for several minutes before they click Save. Conflicts are rare. Which approach fits?

options.v: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE when the form opens, and commit on Save.
Optimistic locking with a version column, checked on Save.
An advisory lock held for the whole session.

why.v: You must never hold a database lock while a person thinks. A version check needs no lock until the write.
